Targets

Each target is a spending level and a withdrawal rate. Set the level as a multiple of your own spending, or as an absolute figure — the FIRE community defines lean, chubby and fat by absolute annual spending, so a multiple of your spending can carry a name it has not earned. Part-time income is the barista FI lever: it reduces what the portfolio has to cover.

Cone is in today’s real (inflation-adjusted) dollars. The cone is a sensitivity range, not a probability. It re-runs the same projection at ±2 percentage points on your real return — it is not a chance of success, and it does not model sequence-of-returns risk, which explains most of the variation in what a portfolio can actually sustain. Healthcare & income thresholds

Before 65 there is no Medicare, and the premium tax credit that pays most of a marketplace plan disappears entirely one dollar past 400% of the poverty line. Below the poverty line in a state that has not expanded Medicaid there is nothing either. Both edges are worth knowing before you pick a retirement income.

$/yr

This is not your spending. Drawing $60,000 from a Roth is about $0 of taxable income; the same $60,000 from a traditional 401(k) is $60,000; from a taxable account only the gain counts. Working that out from your actual balances needs per-account cost basis, which this app does not model yet — so it asks rather than guessing.

Single Married, jointly
Married, jointly: brackets, deduction, and thresholds switch to MFJ. Deductions below are yours only — Social Security is computed per person from the wages you each enter.
What counts as household vs. per-person
Enter only your own 401(k), HSA, medical/dental/vision premiums, employer match, and bonus — there's no separate spouse field, so a spouse's own contributions will be treated as yours. Add'l-Medicare (0.9%) uses a combined $250k household threshold, not a per-person one.
$/yr

Your HSA and medical/dental/vision deductions reduce only your own wage base, not your spouse's. Since Social Security and Medicare are figured from each person's own wage base, which box the same income goes into can change your payroll tax total — income tax stays the same either way.

Changing jobs mid-year

Your annual limits do not reset when you change employer — what you already deferred eats the new job's room — but the §415(c) total-additions cap does reset, because it follows the employer rather than you. Add the wait before you can contribute again and the question stops being "what should I elect" and becomes "can I still get there at all". That is what this answers.

Progress to FI (log where you stand — history starts today)

Each entry stores your net worth and the FI number as it stands right now, so a later change of plan cannot rewrite what you were aiming at. Nothing before your first entry can be shown — the old targets were never recorded, and inventing them would draw a plan you never had.

Ventures — earning back what you invest in yourself

Track a side venture — a course, a certification, equipment — against the money it earns. List what you put in, link its money (a tag you use below, or a dedicated account), and watch how long until it pays for itself.

No ventures yet — track a course, cert, or gear against what it earns back.
Investments to earn back (the course, the gear — typed here, not tagged as transactions):
Two rules keep this honest. (1) List the course and equipment here as investments — the money you want back. (2) Tag every dollar the venture earns and spends (client payments, vials, room rent, insurance) in the ledger below — or link a dedicated account so everything on it counts automatically. Don't tag the course or equipment purchase — it's already counted here. Miss a running cost and your return will look better than it really is. All figures are pre-tax cash payback — venture profit is self-employment income (SE + income tax owed at filing, plus WA B&O if you move) — talk to a professional before acting on "paid back".
